title: Trace cache replaces conventional L1 instruction cache
decision: Store decoded IA-32 micro-ops in a 12K-µop trace cache rather than a conventional L1 instruction cache; the IA-32 decoder is used only on trace-cache miss.
alternatives_or_rejected: Conventional L1 I-cache holding x86 instruction bytes — not-stated-in-paper whether explicitly argued against
rationale: Eliminates decode latency from the main execution loop and stores µops in program-flow (trace) order, increasing delivered instruction bandwidth to the execution core and aiding recovery from mispredicted branches.
outcome: Trace cache achieves hit rate comparable to an 8–16 KB I-cache while bypassing decode; on miss, instructions are fetched from L2 and decoded.
weakest_point: Exact wording of the hit-rate comparison and whether the paper explicitly frames a conventional I-cache as a rejected alternative

title: Very deep (20-stage) pipeline to maximize clock frequency
where_in_paper: Overview of the NetBurst Microarchitecture / Hyper-Pipelined Technology
decision: Deepen pipeline to ~20 stages (vs. ~10 in P6) by simplifying each stage's work, trading higher branch-mispredict penalty for substantially higher achievable clock frequency.
alternatives_or_rejected: Shallower pipeline with more work per stage — not-stated-in-paper whether explicitly weighed
rationale: Simplified stage logic enables much higher clock rates; at 0.18 µm this allowed Pentium 4 to reach 1.5 GHz at introduction versus ~1 GHz limits for P6-based designs at the same process.
outcome: Pentium 4 introduced at 1.5 GHz (November 2000); deep pipeline combined with enhanced branch prediction to mitigate mispredict penalty.
weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly states the pipeline depth as a weighed decision against a shallower alternative, or simply describes it as a feature

title: Double-pumped (2× clocked) ALUs — Rapid Execution Engine
decision: Implement two ALUs and two AGUs that operate at twice the core clock frequency, executing one µop per half-cycle (rising and falling edge).
alternatives_or_rejected: Single-speed ALUs running at core clock — not-stated-in-paper whether explicitly considered
rationale: To compensate for the longer pipeline's per-instruction latency and deliver high integer throughput; at 1.5 GHz core clock the ALUs effectively operate at 3 GHz, providing up to 6 µops/cycle peak issue bandwidth.
outcome: Four double-speed execution ports enable up to 6 µops per cycle to be dispatched; this offsets the IPC penalty of the deep pipeline for integer-heavy code.
weakest_point: Exact distribution of double-speed vs slow ALU and whether the paper frames this explicitly as a trade-off decision

title: 400 MHz system bus via quad-pumping
decision: Use a 100 MHz external bus clock quad-pumped to deliver 400 MHz effective data rate, paired with dual-channel PC800 RDRAM for 3.2 GB/s peak bandwidth.
alternatives_or_rejected: Traditional single-data-rate front-side bus synchronized to memory clock — not-stated-in-paper
rationale: Existing FSB speeds could not satisfy the bandwidth demands of the high-frequency core; quad-pumping decouples effective bus frequency from the physical pin clock.
outcome: 400 MHz system bus delivers ~3× the bandwidth of the 133 MHz Pentium III FSB (1.06 GB/s → 3.2 GB/s).
weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly presents this as a design decision with rejected alternatives, or as a feature description
